The lawsuit came after an Easter email on April 5 that said \"\"He is risen,\"\" which went to about 100,000 employees, and a Christmas message sent on December 23.\n\nThompson wrote that the messages \"\"go too far\"\" and \"\"suggest acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure.\"\" She also said \"\"the good faith intentions of the Secretary are not the issue here.\"\"\n\nThe order does not stop Rollins from sharing her faith. It stops her from using her position to pressure the people who work for her. The judge threw out the Administrative Procedure Act claims but kept the constitutional claim alive.\",\"\",\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/woodspan1967/post-images/main/images/break-the-spin/2026-11-20/bts-20261120-01.jpg\",\"\",\"USDA fired back, calling the case \"\"a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary,\"\" according to AP. The agency is weighing an appeal.\n\nHere is the real question. Two holiday emails, one on Easter and one at Christmas, now sit at the center of a federal court fight over the Establishment Clause. Supporters of the secretary say a greeting is not a command. The employees who sued, backed by a union with more than 19,000 members, say a message from the boss is never just a greeting.\n\nWhichever way an appeals court goes, this one is going to be argued for a long time.\n\nOne detail stands out. The judge said Rollins's good intentions were not the issue. That is the whole fight in a sentence: what a secretary means by a greeting versus how it lands on an employee who answers to her. That is the line the courts are now being asked to draw.\",\"5\",\"\",\"\"\r\n\"\",\"New York's mayor says Rikers Island will finally close. The timeline and the price tag tell a different story.\n\nMayor Zohran Mamdani announced Friday that the jail will close by 2032, replaced by four smaller borough jails. Brooklyn is slated for 2029, the Bronx and Queens for 2031, and Manhattan for 2032. \"\"It is time to finally close Rikers Island,\"\" he said.\n\nThe city's own law required Rikers to close by 2027. AP reports the city is \"\"all but certain\"\" to miss that deadline, which puts the new date about five years late.\n\nThe population is the next problem. Roughly 6,000 people are held at Rikers today, and the plan targets about 4,500. Daily Wire reports the project's cost has grown from about $8.7 billion to about $16 billion. Other outlets cite lower figures, and Breitbart notes Mamdani has not named a funding source.\",\"\",\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/woodspan1967/post-images/main/images/break-the-spin/2026-11-20/bts-20261120-02.jpg\",\"\",\"Reading the plan closely, it depends on a lot of things going right. The jail population has to drop by roughly a quarter. Four new jails have to be built on schedule, in boroughs where neighbors have fought every one of them. And the money has to come from somewhere.\n\nIn the meantime, more than 50 people have died in custody at Rikers since 2022. Even supporters of closing the jail say the city needs a backup plan if the buildings run late.\n\nEveryone agrees Rikers has been a disaster. A plan that misses its legal deadline by five years, costs nearly double the first estimate and has no named funding source is a different thing than a plan that works.\",\"5\",\"\",\"\"\r\n\"\",\"President Trump's planned triumphal arch just lost a second round in federal court.\n\nOn Friday, Judge Leonie Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia granted an injunction blocking construction. The suit was filed October 8 by the Arlington County Board. According to Politico, she told the government: \"\"You don't have congressional approval for this project.\"\" The order has no expiration date.\n\nIt is the second judge to step in. Judge Tanya Chutkan in Washington blocked construction on November 6, and that order was extended to December 3.\n\nThe arch is planned for Memorial Circle, at the Virginia end of Memorial Bridge. The Justice Department said it will appeal.\",\"\",\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/woodspan1967/post-images/main/images/break-the-spin/2026-11-20/bts-20261120-03.jpg\",\"\",\"Supporters argue Congress approved a monument at the site more than a century ago, and that the planning commission has already voted its approval. Judges so far have not agreed that this is enough for a project of this size.\n\nFor the White House, the timing matters. Every week the arch sits in court is another week without construction, and two federal courts in two jurisdictions now stand in the way. Chutkan sits in the District of Columbia and Brinkema in Virginia, so the arch is now tied up on both sides of the Potomac. The injunction from Virginia has no end date, which means the administration cannot simply wait out a short pause the way it might with a two-week order.\n\nExpect an appeal. Whether an appeals court sees the old congressional approval the way the administration does will decide whether this arch is ever built.\n\nWe left out the dollar figure on purpose. Reports put the cost anywhere from over $100 million to $1 billion, and nobody has pinned it down.\",\"5\",\"\",\"\"\r\n\"\",\"President Trump has explained why his National Cyber Director is gone, and he did not soften it.\n\nAsked why he fired Sean Cairncross, Trump said: \"\"Because I didn't think that person was good enough.\"\" Cairncross took office August 4, 2025 and served about 15 months. Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies is now acting director.\n\nThe firing came after a rough stretch of tech outages that hit airports, banks and other systems. Trump rejected the idea that they added up to a pattern. \"\"They were all separate events,\"\" he said.\n\nReports differed on whether Cairncross was pushed or left, and Fox News said the exact departure date was unclear. Trump's own answer settles the question of whether he was fired.\",\"\",\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/woodspan1967/post-images/main/images/break-the-spin/2026-11-20/bts-20261120-04.jpg\",\"\",\"Cairncross was confirmed 59 to 35 in the Senate and was the President's top adviser on national cybersecurity strategy. Critics noted at his nomination that he came from the RNC and had little cyber experience.\n\nHere is the part worth watching. Trump says the outages were separate events, yet he also fired the person in charge of defending against them. Both things can be true, but only one of them explains why the job suddenly opened.\n\nTrump also asked Congress for $50 billion to modernize air traffic control. With the cyber director's chair now held by an acting official, the administration has a lot riding on getting the next pick right. The job exists to coordinate cybersecurity across federal agencies, so an empty chair during a run of outages is not a small thing. Whoever Trump names next will take over with the outage questions still unanswered and a $50 billion air traffic control request in front of Congress.\",\"5\",\"\",\"\"\r\n"
